question: Joining the carboxyl end of one residue to the nitrogen end of the next, a _____ is planar and cannot rotate, which limits the shapes a chain can fold into.
questions: The ribosome makes each _____ at a centre built of RNA rather than protein, so the central reaction of protein synthesis is catalysed by a ribozyme.
Chains of amino acids must have existed before ribosomes did, so how the first _____ was made without one is still an open question about life's origin.
abstract:
A peptide bond joins the amino group of one amino acid to the carboxyl group of another, and a chain of them is a polypeptide, usually hundreds or thousands of residues long. Such a chain has two unlike ends, an amino or N terminus and a carboxyl or C terminus, and it is both built and written from the N end to the C end. The bond itself is planar and permits no rotation, while the other two backbone bonds each residue contributes do rotate, so the chain behaves as a run of rigid plates hinged between them. That constraint, together with the requirement that no two atoms overlap, severely restricts the conformations a chain can take, although a long one can still fold in an enormous number of ways. What a protein is, then, is a polypeptide with one particular sequence, a point settled in 1953 when Frederick Sanger worked out the first complete one, for insulin.

In a living cell the bond is made by the ribosome, at the peptidyl transferase centre in its large subunit, which also carries out the hydrolysis that releases a finished chain. That centre is built from ribosomal RNA rather than protein, so the reaction at the heart of protein synthesis is catalysed by a ribozyme. The ribosome is not the only route, and a class of enzymes called peptide aminoacyl-tRNA ligases extends a peptide at its C terminus without any template, adding amino acids the genetic code does not encode. The bond will also form with no enzyme at all, and simulations of an air-water interface have it assembling rapidly there by an isomerisation and elimination route. That last point matters because chains of amino acids had to exist before ribosomes did, and how the bond was first made in a prebiotic world remains unclear.
